Paired user bootstrap preserves each user’s matched outcomes across models. For this benchmark, resample users within each category and recompute the equal-weight four-category macro difference. Its interpretation is conditional on fitted models and observed candidates: it does not capture training-seed variability, fresh negative draws, split uncertainty, or generalization to other datasets. Independence and representativeness of users remain assumptions. With 200 users/category, one changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points; few discordant users can make intervals unstable or degenerate. These are benchmark-specific implications of [paired resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/).

Repeated checkpoint and hyperparameter selection on the same users and candidates can overfit validation noise. Fixed candidates improve comparability but do not eliminate selection bias; bootstrapping the selected winner’s outcomes does not account for the adaptive search that selected it. A nominal 95% interval therefore lacks automatic post-selection coverage. [Cawley and Talbot](https://jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) show that selection overfitting can rival reported algorithm differences. Within the fixed evaluator and compute budget, prespecify comparisons and stopping rules, record all attempts, and treat validation intervals as exploratory; reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation.

HR@10 against 99 negatives measures ranking within 100 candidates. It cannot establish full-catalog HR@10 improvement: sampled metrics can reverse model order even in expectation, and tighter user-bootstrap intervals cannot remove this sampling bias. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) establish this limitation. Report gains explicitly as fixed-candidate sampled validation gains; full-catalog recommendation quality remains unverified.
